name: Śailaputrī
story: This is Pārvatī as the daughter of Himavat, the mountain king. Her story follows Satī’s death and rebirth as Pārvatī, who returns to Śiva. She comes first in the nine forms. Look for the bull, the trident, and the lotus in her picture.
alt: Śailaputrī seated on a bull, holding a trident and lotus, in a Kolkata Durga Puja sculpture.

name: Brahmacāriṇī
story: Here Pārvatī is the ascetic: she chooses a life of discipline and long penance in her resolve to marry Śiva. The prayer beads and water pot belong to that life. Her story is about staying with a purpose, even when it takes time and asks a lot of her.
alt: A metal relief of Brahmacāriṇī holding prayer beads and a water pot, from Jaipur.

name: Candraghaṇṭā
story: In one wedding story, Śiva arrives with a frightening procession, and Pārvatī takes this powerful form before asking him to appear more gently. The crescent on her forehead gives her the moon-bell name. Her many weapons belong to her role as a protector.
alt: A many-armed Candraghaṇṭā with weapons, seated on a large cat in a Kolkata Durga Puja sculpture.

name: Kūṣmāṇḍā
meaning: The one who brings the universe into being
story: Her creation story starts in darkness. With a smile, Kūṣmāṇḍā brings forth the cosmic egg from which the universe takes shape. She is associated with the sun and its energy. The Kavacham names her here; that larger creation story comes from the traditions around her.
alt: Kūṣmāṇḍā with several arms and a discus, seated on a large cat in a Kolkata Durga Puja sculpture.

name: Skandamātā
story: Skanda is another name for Kārttikeya, the son of Śiva and Pārvatī. This form shows her holding him as a child. His story leads to the defeat of the demon Tāraka. In her picture, the child is the detail that makes the mother-and-son relationship easy to recognize.
alt: Skandamātā holding the many-headed child Skanda, seated on a lion in a Kolkata Durga Puja sculpture.

name: Kātyāyanī
meaning: The warrior linked to sage Kātyāyana
story: This is the warrior form associated with defeating Mahiṣāsura, the buffalo demon. In one account, the gods’ combined power takes form at sage Kātyāyana’s hermitage, giving her this name. The lion and sword make that part of her story visible.
alt: Kātyāyanī holding a sword and seated on a lion in a Kolkata Durga Puja sculpture.

name: Kālarātrī
story: Kālarātrī is one of the fiercest forms in this group. Devotional accounts describe her driving away demons and fear; she is also called Śubhaṅkarī, the one who brings good. The donkey is a useful detail to look for. Her name returns later when the prayer turns to the body.
alt: Kālarātrī seated on a donkey, with weapons and a raised hand, in a Kolkata Durga Puja sculpture.

name: Mahāgaurī
story: One account connects this form to Pārvatī bathing in the Gaṅgā and the emergence of Kauśikī, who goes on to fight Śumbha and Niśumbha. Mahāgaurī is usually shown in white, riding a bull. The stories vary; this is one way to place the name rather than a single definitive account.
alt: Mahāgaurī seated on a bull with a trident and raised hand in a Kolkata Durga Puja sculpture.

name: Siddhidātrī
story: She closes the group of nine. Siddhis are spiritual attainments or powers, and one legend says she grants eight of them to Śiva. She is also linked to Ardhanārīśvara, the form joining Śiva and Pārvatī. Her image is often lotus-seated, with a discus, conch, mace, and lotus.
alt: Siddhidātrī seated on a lotus, holding a discus, conch, mace, and lotus, in a Kolkata Durga Puja sculpture.
